Senses.PreferredTarget: the two halls fight over the cat
AlternateTargets: the two halls dispute the cat
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “the two halls fight over the cat.” The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 29 allowlisted texts; expanded forms specify “the east and west halls.” In the Chan record it is the opening formula and a short name for Nanquan's cat case. The monks of the two halls dispute a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” no one answers, and he cuts it. When Zhaozhou returns, Nanquan recounts the event; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head and leaves, and Nanquan says that had Zhaozhou been present, he would have saved the cat. Later records quote the formula before asking what should have been said, composing verses on the case, or giving prose comments. The exact headword names the dispute that occasions the case; it is not a separate event from “Nanquan cuts the cat.” Elsewhere the corpus explicitly asks why Nanquan cut the cat if killing living beings is a major precept, but no occurrence of this exact formula states Nanquan's reason.
Senses.Note: The explicit precept question belongs to the linked cat-cutting family and is anchored under “cut the cat” (斬猫) and “Nanquan cuts the cat” (南泉斬猫), whose headwords it contains. It is not duplicated here as a headword-free occurrence. The corpus alternates the two graphs for “cat” (貓 and 猫) and often adds “east and west” (東西).

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉東西兩堂爭貓兒，泉來堂內，提起貓兒云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻。」大眾下語皆不契泉意，當時即斬卻貓兒子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's record preserves the east-and-west-halls opening and Nanquan's demand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因兩堂爭貓，乃提起云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉便斬之。趙州自外至，泉舉前話，州脫草履安頭上而出，泉云：「子若在，即救得貓兒也。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later recorded-sayings collection gives the full dispute, cutting, and Zhaozhou sequel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日兩堂爭貓，泉提起貓云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉斬貓為兩段。南泉舉問趙州，州脫鞋戴出，泉云：「子在，救得貓兒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's verse-commentary collection restates the entire case before its verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日兩堂爭貓，泉提起貓，云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉斬貓為兩段。南泉舉問趙州，州脫草鞋戴出，泉云：「子在救得貓兒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Boshan Wuyi's collected comments quote the event as a public case before commenting on it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉禪師因東西兩堂爭貓兒，遂提起貓兒示眾，云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻也。」眾無對，泉便斬卻。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guxue Zhe's record introduces a verse with the east-and-west-halls narration.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "afflictions are awakening" (煩惱即菩提). The phrase uses the copula-like "are" (即) where inherited Buddhist vocabulary would ordinarily oppose afflictions (煩惱) and awakening (菩提); Chan records both state that reversal and police its recitation. Yuan Cheng answers the direct question "What does 'afflictions are awakening' mean?" (煩惱即菩提，何謂也) by rendering awakening as "knowing and perceiving" (知覺). He then says that because awakening does not differ from afflictions, being confused about awakening is called affliction, while knowing affliction is awakening; he adds that storing up that knowing itself is then called affliction. Dahui records the phrase twice as a conditional speech boundary: he rebukes people who force the proposition while their conduct contradicts their talk, and later says only after "breaking through" (打得徹) may one say it. The Record of Ancient Venerables likewise says beginners commonly claim to understand it as a uniform equalized view, then notes that their ordinary-and-holy and still-and-noisy distinctions remain twofold. The distinctive Chan use is not a flat identity statement: the corpus turns the inherited opposition into an equation while its masters directly challenge merely repeating that equation.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 48 hits in 28 allowlisted texts; 17 are in the Mirror Record. The curated evidence foregrounds Yuan Cheng's direct question-and-answer definition and two independent warnings against treating the formula as verbal understanding. 'Awakening' translates the passage's own gloss 'knowing and perceiving'; the entry reports only the predicates these Chan passages state.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又問：煩惱即菩提，何謂也？師曰：梵語菩提，此云知覺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuan Cheng receives the direct definition question and renders awakening in Chinese as knowing and perceiving.

Occurrences.Kwic: 以菩提不異煩惱，迷菩提為煩惱。以煩惱不異菩提，知煩惱即菩提。葢知之為言，覺也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuan Cheng continues the answer with the paired predicates of being confused about awakening and knowing affliction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又於隨順境中。彊說道理。謂煩惱即菩提。無明即大智。步步行有。口口談空。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui rebukes forced recitation of the phrase alongside 'ignorance is great wisdom,' contrasting conduct at every step with emptiness on every tongue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打得徹了。方可說煩惱即菩提無明即大智。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's next passage makes breaking through the stated condition for saying the two equations.

Occurrences.Kwic: 閙中得靜則井邑成山林煩惱即菩提眾生成正覺此語初心學人例道得會得作一種平等知見
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Ancient Venerables lists the phrase among sayings beginners claim to understand as one equalized view, before testing that claim against remaining distinctions.
